parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State an experimental phenomenon that provides evidence for:

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem: A particle of matter moves with momentum $p$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: State the equation that gives the effective wavelength $\lambda$ of the particle. State the name of any other symbols used.
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the two sides of duality - the wave side is represented by wavelength $\lambda$ and the particle side by momentum $p$. How are they inversely linked?
Hint 2: Recall the universal quantum constant that connects energy and frequency for photons, $E = hf$. The same constant links $\lambda$ and $p$ for matter.
parts.proper_answer: $\lambda = h / p$ where $h$ is the Planck constant.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Linking Wave and Particle Properties**
For any moving matter particle, its effective wavelength gets shorter when its momentum gets larger. The link is very simple and inverse.

Step 2: **Stating the Relation**
$$\lambda = \frac{h}{p}$$
Here $\lambda$ is the effective wavelength of the particle, $p$ is its momentum, and $h$ is the Planck constant, $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: State the name given to the wavelength of the moving particle.
hints: Hint 1: Think of the French physicist who first proposed in his PhD thesis that all moving matter has an associated wavelength.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Naming the Matter Wave**
The wavelength $\lambda = h/p$ associated with a moving particle is called the de Broglie wavelength, after Louis de Broglie who proposed matter waves.

parts.label: (c)
parts.part_stem: Electrons are accelerated from rest through a potential difference (p.d.) of $4.8\text{kV}$.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: Show that the final speed of the electrons is $4.1 \times 10^7\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
hints: Hint 1: Start from energy conservation - the electrical work done on the electron from rest becomes its kinetic energy. What are the expressions for those two energies?
Hint 2: Convert $4.8 \text{ kV}$ to volts and use $m = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$ and $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ to solve for $v$ before squaring or rooting.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Equating Electrical Work to Kinetic Energy**
An electron starting from rest gains kinetic energy equal to the work done by the field. That gives a clean energy balance with no wasted energy.

Step 2: **Calculating the Speed**
$$\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = eV$$
$$v = \sqrt{\frac{2eV}{m}}$$
With $V = 4.8 \text{ kV} = 4800 \text{ V}$:
$$v = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 4800}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}}}$$
$$v = \sqrt{1.69 \times 10^{15}} = 4.1 \times 10^7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the effective wavelength of a beam of electrons moving at the speed in (c)(i).
hints: Hint 1: Use the matter-wave relation from (b) and write momentum $p$ in terms of the electron mass and the speed found in (c)(i).
Hint 2: Insert $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$, $m = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$ and $v = 4.1 \times 10^7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, checking powers of ten carefully.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Applying the Matter-Wave Equation to the Electron**
Momentum of the electron is $p = mv$, so the de Broglie wavelength becomes $\lambda = h/mv$. Faster electrons have larger momentum and so a shorter wavelength.

Step 2: **Substituting Numbers**
$$\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}$$
$$\lambda = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 4.1 \times 10^7}$$
$$\lambda = 1.8 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}$$

parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think of an experiment where light knocks electrons out of a metal instantly, and where changing brightness alone cannot explain what happens.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why Light Must Sometimes Act As Particles**
Wave theory predicts that bright light of any colour should eventually give electrons enough energy to escape. In reality electrons are only emitted if the frequency is above a threshold, no matter how intense low-frequency light is. This can only be explained if light arrives in packets called photons, each with energy $E = hf$.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think of the classic wave behaviour you see with light passing through a narrow gap or crystal - which experiment shows electrons doing the same thing?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why Electrons Must Sometimes Act As Waves**
If electrons were only particles they could not interfere or diffract. When a beam of electrons passes through a thin graphite film or crystal lattice, a pattern of rings is seen on a screen. That is diffraction, a property only waves show, so moving matter must have a wave nature.
